title: Elasticity: why solids stretch and spring back

sources.title: OpenStax: Stress, strain and elastic modulus

chapters.title: Elastic does not simply mean easy to stretch
chapters.formula: Elastic: recovers after unloading; plastic: permanent deformation
points: Elasticity describes recovery after the load is removed.
The proportional limit and elastic limit are different concepts.
chapters.script: Welcome back. We have often treated objects as perfectly rigid. Real solids can change shape under a force, even when the change is too small to notice. Pull gently on a metal wire and it becomes slightly longer. Remove the force, and within its elastic range it returns to its original length. That recovery is what elasticity means. It does not simply mean easy to stretch. A material may be stiff, meaning difficult to deform, and still recover elastically. If a load leaves a permanent change after removal, that is plastic deformation. Imagine bending a paper clip gently, then bending it much farther. The small bend may recover; the larger bend may remain. We will use a simpler model: a uniform wire stretched slowly along its length, with small deformation and negligible self weight. There are two limits to keep separate. Below the proportional limit, stress is proportional to strain. The elastic limit concerns whether the material fully recovers after unloading. A material can show nonlinear yet recoverable behaviour, so these limits are not automatically identical. In JEE questions, read the stated regime before choosing an equation. Today we will calculate how much a wire stretches and how much energy that stretch stores.

chapters.title: Stress shares the load; strain measures the change
chapters.formula: Stress = F/A; longitudinal strain = extension/original length
points: Use the tensile force across a section, not the sum of opposite end forces.
Stress has unit pascal, or N/m squared; strain is dimensionless.
100 N over 1 mm squared gives stress 100 million Pa.
chapters.script: Suppose two wires carry the same pulling force, but one is thicker. The force alone does not describe how intensely each wire is loaded. Stress divides the tensile force by the cross sectional area. Spreading the same force over a larger area gives less stress. In static tension, equal opposite forces at the ends balance the wire overall. Do not add their magnitudes and use twice the force in the stress formula. Use the tension transmitted through a cross section. The unit of stress is newtons per square metre, called the pascal. Watch the area conversion: one square millimetre is one millionth of a square metre, because both length dimensions are converted. A hundred newtons acting over one square millimetre therefore gives one hundred million pascals of stress. Now describe the deformation. Longitudinal strain is extension divided by original length. If a two metre wire extends by one millimetre, convert that extension to zero point zero zero one metres. Divide by two to get zero point zero zero zero five. Strain has no unit because it is a ratio of lengths. The extension is one millimetre, but the strain is not one millimetre. Keeping those quantities separate prevents a very common error.

chapters.title: Young's modulus and a complete wire problem
points: The equation assumes small, linear elastic stretching.
F = 100 N; L = 2 m; A = 1 mm squared; Y = 200 billion Pa.
chapters.script: In the linear elastic region, longitudinal stress equals Young's modulus times longitudinal strain. Young's modulus, written capital Y, describes the material's resistance to this deformation. Because strain is dimensionless, Y has the same unit as stress: pascals. Rearrange the equation carefully. Stress is force over area, and strain is extension over original length. Solving for extension gives force times original length, divided by area times Young's modulus. Let us solve our wire example completely. The force is one hundred newtons, the original length is two metres, and the area is one square millimetre. The material's Young's modulus is two hundred billion pascals. First convert the area to one millionth of a square metre. The numerator, force times length, is two hundred. The denominator, area times modulus, is two hundred thousand. Dividing gives zero point zero zero one metres, or one millimetre. Pause and check it another way. Stress is one hundred million pascals; divide by two hundred billion to get strain zero point zero zero zero five. Multiply by two metres to recover the same extension. We assumed the load remains within the proportional region. A formula cannot tell us that the material is safe without information about its limits.

chapters.title: JEE comparisons: length, thickness and material
chapters.formula: Extension is proportional to FL/(AY); for a circular wire A = pi r squared
points: Same F, A and Y: doubling L doubles extension.
Same F, L and Y: doubling radius quarters extension.
Doubling length and radius together halves extension.
chapters.script: Now use the extension equation without repeatedly substituting large numbers. Under the same force, two wires of the same material and cross section have extension proportional to original length. Double the length and the extension doubles. Why? The same strain acts over twice as much original length. Next, keep length and material unchanged but double the radius of a circular wire. Predict the extension. Take a moment. Area is pi times radius squared, so doubling the radius makes the area four times larger. The extension becomes one quarter as large, not one half. If both length and radius double, the length contributes a factor of two while the area contributes a factor of four in the denominator. The new extension is half the old extension. Finally, compare materials using identical force, length, and area. A larger Young's modulus produces a smaller extension. It is the material stiffness that changes here. The stiffness of the whole wire also depends on geometry. Writing force equals k times extension gives an effective spring constant k equal to area times Young's modulus divided by length. A longer wire has smaller k, even though its material has exactly the same Young's modulus. This distinction is useful whenever a JEE question changes the dimensions but not the material.

chapters.title: Stored energy and the graph check
chapters.formula: Stored energy = (1/2) F x = (1/2) k x squared
points: For slow loading from zero in the linear elastic range, force rises with extension.
100 N final force and 1 mm extension store 0.05 J.
Area under a force-extension graph is work; its slope is wire stiffness k.
chapters.script: Stretching the wire stores elastic energy. Why is the energy not simply final force times extension? During slow loading from zero, the force is initially zero and increases as the wire stretches. In the linear elastic model, the force extension graph is a straight line through the origin. Work is the area under that graph. The area is a triangle, so stored energy is one half times final force times final extension. Equivalently, it is one half k times extension squared. For our wire, the final force is one hundred newtons and the extension is one millimetre, or zero point zero zero one metres. Multiply one half by one hundred by zero point zero zero one. The stored energy is zero point zero five joules. A sudden application of a constant load is a different dynamical problem; do not assume that all its work is stored at the static extension. One more graph distinction matters. On a force versus extension graph, slope is the wire's spring constant. On a stress versus strain graph, the initial linear slope is Young's modulus. Before solving, identify the axes. Your final checklist is original length, cross sectional area in square metres, force transmitted through the wire, and the linear elastic assumption. Shear, bulk compression, fluids, and thermal expansion need their own lessons.

quiz.question: A solid fully returns to its original shape after unloading. This describes:
quiz.explanation: Elastic recovery is return to the original shape after removal of the load; it does not mean easy deformation.

quiz.question: A wire carries tension 100 N over area 1 mm squared. Its tensile stress is:
quiz.explanation: 1 mm squared = 0.000001 m squared. Stress = 100/0.000001 = 100 million Pa, using the tension once.

quiz.question: A 2 m wire has area 1 mm squared and Y = 200 billion Pa. Under 100 N in the linear regime, its extension is:
For the same material and tensile force, both the length and radius of a circular wire double. Extension becomes:
quiz.explanation: Extension is proportional to L/r squared. The ratio is 2/4 = 1/2.

quiz.question: A linearly elastic wire is slowly stretched from zero load to 100 N and 1 mm extension. Stored energy is:
quiz.explanation: Energy is the triangular area under the force-extension graph: 0.5 x 100 x 0.001 = 0.05 J.
